title: Not by birth (383–390)
hook: not by birth is one a brahmana, but by conduct; cut the stream, be bold

segments.voice: Yesterday, the young monk, and your line: young and awake. What ordinary thing did you do wholeheartedly? Day two hundred twenty-five, a new week, and the last chapter of the Dhammapada.

Every society has words of honor that come with a family name. Old money. Good family. A title you inherit. And most of us have met someone with every advantage of birth who behaved badly, and someone with none of them who was simply noble. The last chapter of the Dhammapada takes one of the most honored words of its world and asks a sharp question: what actually earns it? The chapter is forty-one verses long, the longest in the book, and nearly every verse ends the same way. Today: not by birth.
screen: `WORDS OF HONOR BY BIRTH.` → `NOBLE WITHOUT ANY ADVANTAGE.` → `WHAT ACTUALLY EARNS IT?`

segments.voice: Today's word is brahmana, in Sanskrit brahmin. In the Buddha's India, brahmins were the hereditary priestly class, the keepers of the Vedas and the sacred rites, and many were honored teachers; brahmins came to the Buddha as questioners, and many became his students. The Buddha didn't throw the word away. He kept it as a word of honor, and changed what it takes to earn it. In a sutta called the discourse on the outcast, he puts it directly: no one is an outcast by birth, and no one is a brahmin by birth. By deeds one becomes an outcast, and by deeds one becomes a brahmin. The Dhammapada's last chapter is built on that idea. It opens with courage: cut off the stream of craving, be bold, drive away desire. When you understand how things come to an end, it says, you know the unmade. Then a lovely verse about light. The sun shines by day, the moon by night, the warrior shines in armor, the brahmana in meditation; but the Buddha shines day and night. And a verse full of wordplay. One is called a brahmana because he has put evil away, a samana, a renunciant, because he lives in calm, and a pabbajita, one gone forth, because he has sent his own impurities away. The chapter's refrain, which runs through all four days of this chapter, is: him I call a brahmana. Each verse fills it with conduct: patience, gentleness, truth, freedom from clinging. Nobility, in this chapter, is something you do.
screen: `BRAHMANA — THE PRIESTLY CLASS.` · `BY DEEDS, NOT BY BIRTH.` · `SUN, MOON, WARRIOR, BRAHMANA.` · `HIM I CALL A BRAHMANA.` · then, large: `NOT BY BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Let go, for these two minutes, of every label that came with you: your family name, your job title, where you're from, what you own. None of them are needed to breathe. Notice what's left: this breath, this body, this attention. Now think of one small, good thing you could do today that nobody will ever know about. Just picture it. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Brahmana. In the Buddha's world a priestly class by birth; in this chapter, a title earned only by conduct.
Your line: not by birth. Today, do something noble quietly, one kindness with no name attached, and let no one find out. Day two hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the brahmana chapter and the Vasala Sutta to teach that worth comes from conduct, not birth; in Theravada countries the chapter's verses are often chanted, and its refrain is well known.

match.prompt: match each word in today's verses.
pairs: in this chapter, earned by conduct

myth: the Buddha threw away the word brahmana
he kept it as a word of honor and said it's earned by deeds.
the last chapter of the Dhammapada is its longest
many brahmins became the Buddha's students
brahmins came to him as questioners, and many stayed as students.

fork.setup: someone of high birth behaves cruelly; someone of low birth behaves nobly. who does this chapter call a brahmana?
options: neither; it depends on their family.
fork.reveal: the Buddha said no one is a brahmin by birth; by deeds one becomes a brahmin.

original.note: Pali brāhmaṇa (Sanskrit brāhmaṇa, 'brahmin'): chapter twenty-six's title and refrain.

trapdoor: what you thought: brahmana just means a member of the priestly caste.
what it means: in this chapter, a title of honor earned only by conduct, not birth.

what a scholar hears: the same teaching appears in the Vasala Sutta (Sn 1.7) and the Vasettha Sutta (Sn 3.9); verse 388 plays on brahmana/bahita-papa (evil put away) and pabbajita/pabbajayam (sending away impurity).

notes: All verses paraphrased. The 'not by birth' line is from Sn 1.7 (Vasala Sutta); Dhp 393 (tomorrow) makes the same point.
Description of brahmins in the Buddha's day is kept respectful and historical; a Hindu reader should recognize it. Keeper may wish to review for tone.
Verse 387 (sun, moon, warrior, brahmana, the Buddha shines day and night) and 388's wordplay paraphrased; confirm the etymological puns.
Refrain 'him I call a brahmana' is Müller's phrasing ('Him I call indeed a Brahmana'), used unquoted as a paraphrase.
